g: Young adult and crossover fantasy; mythic romance
sum: Lazlo Strange, an orphan and junior librarian, has spent his life obsessed with the lost city of Weep, whose very name was mysteriously erased from the world’s memory. When a hero from that city arrives seeking scholars and engineers, Lazlo seizes the chance to join the expedition and discovers a city haunted by a floating citadel and by the blue-skinned children of murdered gods.
bg: Laini Taylor published Strange the Dreamer in 2017, and it was a Michael L. Printz Honor Book. Taylor is known for her Daughter of Smoke and Bone trilogy. The story concludes in Muse of Nightmares. It was widely read by adults as well as teenagers.
br: The opening in the library and the journey to Weep is slow, lush and dreamlike; the second half shifts to Sarai, a goddess’s daughter who walks in dreams. The ending is a cliffhanger, so have the sequel ready.
la: Taylor writes ornate, lyrical prose rich with metaphor and invented mythology, and alternates between Lazlo and Sarai to build a romance across enmity and dreams. Library, desert and dream scenes are vividly drawn.
cx: The novel explores the aftermath of atrocity and the inherited trauma of a city liberated from cruel gods, and whether the children of oppressors can be innocent.
th: Dreams and imagination
Lazlo’s imagination is both his gift and his courage.
Inherited trauma
A city still bears the wounds of its past.
Hatred and compassion
Love across enmity challenges a cycle of revenge.
fit: A lush, romantic fantasy duology with a complete arc, pairing well with The Night Circus.
mis: Ornate prose and a slow start may not suit readers who prefer brisk storytelling.
rq: How do Lazlo and Sarai’s dreams connect?
What happened in the city’s past?
dq: Can the children of oppressors be innocent?
How does Taylor’s prose shape the mood?
rel: The Night Circus, another lush romance.

g: Young adult and crossover fantasy; duology conclusion
sum: After the shattering ending of Strange the Dreamer, Lazlo and Sarai face a new reality and a powerful new threat in the citadel above Weep, while the humans below wrestle with fear and vengeance. As old secrets surface and new characters arrive from another world, they must find a way to protect each other and break the cycle of violence.
bg: Laini Taylor published Muse of Nightmares in 2018 to conclude the duology. It expands the world beyond Weep and reveals much about the gods’ origins. The two books together form one long story, best read close together so the first book’s details stay fresh.
br: Read only after Strange the Dreamer; this profile avoids its ending. New viewpoints, including two sisters from elsewhere, are woven in. Expect a long, emotional final third that answers the first book’s mysteries.
la: Taylor continues her lyrical style while widening the story to cosmic mysteries, and turns a villain into a complex, sympathetic character. Moments of humour and tenderness balance the darker material throughout.
cx: The conclusion focuses on healing, forgiveness and the possibility of redemption after trauma. It refuses to make anyone simply a monster, and asks what each survivor needs in order to heal and live alongside former enemies.
th: Forgiveness
Healing requires understanding the pain of one’s enemies as well as one’s own.
Redemption
Even those shaped by cruelty can choose to change.
Love and sacrifice
Love demands courage, honesty and difficult choices from everyone it touches.
fit: Completes the duology with an emotional, satisfying ending. It gives every main character a meaningful ending.
mis: Long and slow in places, with new plot threads some find distracting. Some subplots feel crowded.
rq: What do the new characters reveal?
How does the ending resolve the cycle of violence?

g: Historical fantasy; alternate history of English magic
sum: In 1806, magic has long been a scholarly hobby in England rather than a practical art, until the reclusive Mr Norrell of Hurtfew Abbey demonstrates real magic by making the statues of York Cathedral speak. He brings magic to the aid of the government during the Napoleonic Wars, and takes a gifted, impulsive pupil, Jonathan Strange, whose ambition and curiosity soon threaten their partnership and the boundary with Faerie.
bg: Susanna Clarke spent about ten years writing the novel, published in 2004. It won the Hugo Award and the World Fantasy Award and was adapted for BBC television in 2015. Her later novel Piranesi is already on your list.
br: Very long, with many footnotes containing stories, legends and scholarly asides; enjoy them as part of the fun. The pace is leisurely, and patience is rewarded. The book is divided into three volumes, each named for a magician: Mr Norrell, Jonathan Strange and John Uskglass.
la: Clarke writes in a pastiche of early nineteenth-century prose, like Austen with fairies, full of dry wit, irony and invented scholarship, creating a convincing alternate history. The omniscient narrator is a delight.
cx: The novel mixes real history, including Wellington and the Napoleonic Wars, with invented magical history, and explores class, race and the forgotten magic of the North of England.
th: Rivalry and friendship
Two very different magicians are bound together by magic and pride.
Knowledge and control
Norrell hoards magical knowledge, while Strange wants it shared.
Faerie and danger
The fairy world is beautiful, cruel and alien.
fit: A delightful, immersive companion to Piranesi and The Night Circus on your list.
mis: Its length, slow pace and footnotes can test patience. Others find it their perfect book.
rq: How do Strange and Norrell differ?
What role do the footnotes play?
Who is the gentleman with the thistle-down hair?
dq: What does the novel say about English history?
Why does Clarke write in this style?

sum: In the early 1900s, January Scaller lives as the ward of the wealthy Mr Locke in a mansion full of artefacts, while her father travels the world collecting treasures. When she discovers a mysterious book telling of Doors that lead to other worlds, she begins to uncover the truth about her family, her own power, and the people who want to close the Doors forever.
bg: Alix E. Harrow published her debut novel in 2019; it was a finalist for the Hugo and Nebula awards. Harrow, a former history instructor, later wrote The Once and Future Witches. The novel was praised especially for its love of books and storytelling.
br: The story alternates between January’s narrative and chapters from the book she discovers; both threads converge. Enjoy the love of books and stories that runs through it. Short chapters help the pace.
la: Harrow writes lyrical, warm prose and uses a story-within-a-story structure to celebrate the power of stories and doorways to change the world. Its descriptions of doors and thresholds are especially evocative, and January’s voice is spirited and warm.
cx: Set in an era of empire and colonial collecting, the novel critiques the powerful who want to control change, and centres a mixed-race heroine. Historical details of the period are well researched.
th: Doors and change
Doors bring change, which the powerful fear and try to prevent.
Stories
Reading and writing stories are real acts of power and freedom.
Freedom
January fights to define her own life against those who would control it.
fit: A lyrical, bookish adventure that pairs with The Night Circus and Piranesi. It is a love letter to reading.
mis: Some find the prose overwrought and the pace slow. The villains can feel one-dimensional.
rq: What does the book within the book reveal?
What does January learn about herself?
dq: How does the novel celebrate reading?
